title: Held the line. September 12, 2026.
excerpt: From 21 soldiers who refused to retreat in 1897 to a founder who heard fifty investors say no before Nasdaq said yes, September 12 was about staying in a position everyone else would have abandoned.
bodyHtml:
Every so often, this project's five stories line up around one idea without being planned that way. September 12 was one of those days - the through-line was simple: every story here is about someone who could have reasonably quit, and didn't.

Twenty-one soldiers, a ridge, and no realistic chance of reinforcement

Start with the Battle of Saragarhi, fought on this exact date in 1897. On the Samana Ridge of the North-West Frontier, a garrison of 21 Sikh soldiers from the 36th Sikhs, led by Havildar Ishar Singh, faced a tribal force numbering in the thousands - vastly outnumbered, with no realistic hope of help arriving in time. Every one of them chose to hold the post rather than surrender or retreat. All 21 died. All 21 were posthumously awarded the Indian Order of Merit, the era's highest gallantry honor open to Indian soldiers, and the British Parliament held a rare standing tribute in their memory.

Nearly 130 years later, the Indian Army still marks this date every year as Saragarhi Day - a Regimental Battle Honours Day for the Sikh Regiment, and a state holiday in Punjab since 2017. The standard those 21 soldiers set for holding a position against impossible odds is still the one referenced.

Fifty investors said no, so he built the door instead

Kanwal Rekhi's version of holding the line took decades instead of hours. An IIT Bombay graduate, Rekhi moved to the US in the early 1970s and co-founded Excelan, a Silicon Valley networking hardware company, at a time when almost no Indian founders were raising venture money - reportedly hearing rejection from around fifty investors before finding backing. In 1987, he took Excelan public on Nasdaq: the first Indian-American founder and CEO to take a venture-backed company public on a US stock exchange.

Rekhi didn't stop at his own IPO. He went on to co-found TiE - The Indus Entrepreneurs - now the world's largest network of Indian and South Asian entrepreneurs. One door opening became the reason the next fifty didn't have to fight as hard to get through it.

The infrastructure that never trends, still compounding

India's ports are the least dramatic story of the day, and maybe the most honest one about what "holding the line" looks like at national scale. India's Major Ports handled a record 915.17 million tonnes of cargo this financial year - up 7.06% year-on-year, beating the government's own 904 million tonne target. Cargo on India's national waterways grew even faster, up nearly 50%. Deendayal Port and Paradip Port each moved over 150 million tonnes on their own, and India has now earmarked over $80 billion for port infrastructure through 2035.

Nobody posts about a port on social media. But every export, every import, every factory depending on either one runs through this infrastructure first - the unglamorous groundwork that has to hold, every single day, for everything built on top of it to work.

Money that stays, instead of just passing through

NRI real estate investment tells a quieter version of the same commitment. A decade ago, almost no property buyer in India was from abroad - now nearly one in five is. NRI buyers have gone from roughly 7% of Indian property purchases in 2015 to close to 20% today, nearly tripling in ten years, with Bengaluru and Mumbai as the top two destinations. This is happening alongside record remittances - $135 billion sent home last year, up 14% - giving the diaspora more capital to invest.

A house isn't a quick transaction. It's a twenty-year bet on the place you buy it in, made by people who could have put that money anywhere else in the world, and chose not to.

The scoreboard doesn't record the odds

The smallest story of the day says the quiet part out loud: nobody remembers the odds you were up against - only whether you held the line. The scoreboard rarely records how outnumbered you were, how little backup you had, or how reasonable it would have been to fold. It only records whether you stayed.

Five stories, one day. None of them are the whole picture on their own - the picture is what they add up to.

coverHeadlines: India's ports just moved more cargo in one year than ever before. And they beat their own target doing it.
Twenty one soldiers held a fort against thousands - and won a place in history by losing.
Nobody remembers the odds you were up against - only whether you held the line.
He became the first Indian-American founder to take a company public on Nasdaq - after fifty investors said no.
A decade ago, almost no property buyer in India was from abroad. Now nearly one in five is.
